items.title: Cognitive transparency and trust calibration in explainable AI systems: a psychological model of human-AI decision reliance
items.abstract: Introduction Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is widely expected to improve transparency and support appropriate human reliance on AI-assisted decision-making. However, the psychological processes through which explainability relates to reliance remain insufficiently understood, and explainability, transparency, and trust have largely been examined separately. Objectives This study develops and tests a psychological model of cognitive transparency in which AI explainability, algorithmic transparency, and perceived AI accuracy are associated with human reliance on AI through cognitive understanding, cognitive trust, and trust calibration, with AI literacy as a boundary condition. Methods A cross-sectional online survey was completed by 342 AI users in South Korea in May and June 2026. Each participant evaluated one self-selected AI system that they had personally used; all constructs were measured by self-report. The data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4. Results AI explainability (β = 0.349) and algorithmic transparency (β = 0.297) were positively associated with cognitive understanding. Cognitive understanding (β = 0.388) and, more strongly, perceived AI accuracy (β = 0.492) were associated with cognitive trust. Cognitive trust was associated with trust calibration (β = 0.631), which was associated with human reliance on AI (β = 0.600). All hypothesized indirect effects were significant, and AI literacy strengthened the association between AI explainability and cognitive understanding (β = 0.192). The model explained 36%–54% of the variance in the endogenous constructs and showed medium predictive power. Conclusion The findings are consistent with a sequence in which explainable AI relates to reliance through users’ understanding and trust judgments. Because all constructs were self-reported and measured at a single point in time, the results describe associations among users’ perceptions rather than causal effects, independently verified calibration, or objectively appropriate reliance. The findings suggest that AI developers in domains such as healthcare, education, and finance, where calibrated reliance is critical, should pair user-facing explanations with information about system accuracy and with AI literacy support.

items.title: Context matters in just culture: Translating formal just culture into lived near-miss reporting experience in maritime transportation
items.abstract: In onboard environments characterised by high operational risk, near-miss reporting is an important mechanism for identifying latent risks, preventing accidents and supporting organisational improvement. However, there remains limited empirical understanding of whether the just culture advocated in formal systems can be translated into the lived reporting experience of seafarers who are willing, able and motivated to report near-miss incidents on a sustained basis. To address this issue, this study draws on semi-structured interviews with seafarers and shore-based managers. Six interrelated themes are identified: ease of reporting, motivation to report, trust, reporting independence, feedback and acknowledgement. The findings indicate that near-miss reporting is more likely to occur in organisational contexts where reporting is accessible, safe and worthwhile. Complicated procedures, paperwork burdens and hierarchical pressure weaken seafarers’ willingness to report, whereas simplified procedures, fair management, low exposure communication channels, timely feedback and positive acknowledgement help strengthen reporting willingness and promote experience sharing. This study provides context-specific empirical evidence on how formal just culture is translated into frontline reporting practice and offers practical insights that may inform efforts to improve near-miss reporting, reduce reporting concerns and strengthen closed-loop feedback in comparable organisational or cultural settings.

items.title: CRITICAL EVALUATION OF AI-GENERATED FEEDBACK IN EFL ACADEMIC WRITING
items.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education has created new opportunities for supporting academic writing. AI-powered tools can provide immediate feedback on grammar, vocabulary, sentence structure, and text organisation. However, the availability of automated feedback does not guarantee that learners can evaluate its accuracy or use it effectively. This paper examines the importance of developing EFL learners’ ability to critically evaluate AI-generated feedback through a conceptual analysis of relevant literature. Previous research has investigated learners’ engagement with automated writing evaluation, their responses to ChatGPT-generated suggestions, and the effectiveness of AI feedback in comparison with teacher feedback (Yang et al., 2024; Cengiz et al., 2025; Alnemrat et al., 2025). Building on these studies and the concept of student feedback literacy (Carless & Boud, 2018), the paper proposes a four-stage pedagogical framework: analysing feedback, verifying suggestions, justifying revision decisions, and reflecting on revised texts. The framework emphasises the importance of learner judgement, teacher guidance, and responsible AI use. It may provide a basis for designing EFL academic writing activities in higher education, including the Uzbek educational context. Further empirical research is needed to evaluate its effectiveness in classroom practice. Keywords: artificial intelligence, AI-generated feedback, EFL academic writing, critical evaluation, feedback literacy, writing instruction

items.title: De l'e-gouvernement au gouvernement digital : revue intégrative des trajectoires de maturité et des capacités d'intégration organisationnelle
items.abstract: Résumé La littérature sur l’e-gouvernement s’est longtemps structurée autour de deux questions : le degré de sophistication des services numériques et les facteurs d’adoption par les usagers. Ces approches ont produit des modèles utiles, mais elles rendent imparfaitement compte du passage d’une offre de services en ligne à une transformation durable des organisations publiques. Cet article propose une revue intégrative visant à réexaminer cette transition à partir d’un corpus de 34 articles scientifiques publiés entre 2001 et 2026 dans des revues indexées dans Scopus et/ou Web of Science. L’analyse articule quatre courants : les modèles de maturité, les travaux sur l’adoption et la confiance, la transformation organisationnelle et l’interopérabilité, ainsi que la littérature sur la valeur publique. Trois résultats principaux émergent. Premièrement, la maturité numérique ne peut être assimilée à une trajectoire linéaire : les administrations combinent des niveaux hétérogènes de sophistication des services, d’intégration des données et de transformation interne. Deuxièmement, l’existence d’infrastructures ou de services numériques constitue une condition nécessaire mais non suffisante ; leur appropriation dépend de l’accessibilité, des compétences numériques, de la confiance, de l’utilisabilité et de l’adéquation des canaux. Troisièmement, le passage au gouvernement digital repose surtout sur des capacités organisationnelles d’intégration : leadership, gouvernance du changement, compétences, interopérabilité, coordination interorganisationnelle et apprentissage. Sur cette base, l’article propose un modèle théorique d’intégration stratégique du gouvernement digital reliant fondations sociotechniques, capacités d’appropriation, capacités organisationnelles et création de valeur publique, sous l’effet modérateur du contexte institutionnel et de la capacité administrative. Sept propositions théoriques sont formulées. La contribution consiste à déplacer l’unité d’analyse de la simple maturité technologique vers la capacité d’une administration à intégrer, maintenir et reconfigurer le numérique au service de finalités publiques. Mots clés : e-gouvernement ; gouvernement digital ; transformation numérique publique ; maturité numérique ; capacités organisationnelles ; interopérabilité ; valeur publique. Abstract Research on e-government has long focused on the sophistication of online public services and the determinants of their adoption. Although informative, these perspectives do not fully explain how the digitization of public services becomes sustained organizational transformation. This article presents an integrative review of 34 scientific articles published between 2001 and 2026 in journals indexed in Scopus and/or Web of Science. It brings together four streams of research: digital maturity models; adoption and trust; organizational transformation and interoperability; and public value. Three main findings emerge. First, digital maturity does not follow a necessarily linear trajectory: public administrations may combine sophisticated online services with fragmented data systems and limited internal change. Second, digital infrastructures and online services are necessary but insufficient conditions for effective use, which also depends on accessibility, digital skills, trust, usability, and the suitability of service channels. Third, the transition to digital government relies on organizational integration capabilities, including leadership, change governance, staff competencies, interoperability, interorganizational coordination, and organizational learning. On this basis, the article develops a theoretical model of strategic digital government integration linking sociotechnical foundations, appropriation capabilities, organizational capabilities, and public value creation, with institutional context and administrative capacity as moderating conditions. Seven theoretical propositions are formulated. The contribution is to shift the unit of analysis from technological maturity alone to the capacity of public administrations to integrate, sustain, and reconfigure digital resources in pursuit of public purposes. Keywords: e-government; digital government; public-sector digital transformation; digital maturity; organizational capabilities; interoperability; public value.

items.title: Decision-Making When Computational Complexity Drives Uncertainty
items.abstract: This review summarizes research over the past two decades on human attitudes toward computationally “hard” problems. The focus is on the nature of uncertainty that computational complexity generates because humans do not have the cognitive capacity or the resources (time) to fully resolve the problems. Although decision theorists have traditionally labeled this type of uncertainty “ambiguity,” behavior under computational complexity shows that humans neither deal with it as prescribed in rational decision theory nor simply avoid it as in traditional accounts of ambiguity aversion. Instead, behavior (effort applied and performance reached) exhibits distinct features that can be rationalized using the theory of computational complexity, originally developed for electronic computers. Although the theory cannot decisively tell us which problems are most difficult, it does provide classifications that allow one to predict human performance and effort. The theory also identifies which instances of a problem are more difficult, and human performance and effort appear to align with this identification. Evidence is discussed that humans do not appear to allocate cognitive effort ex ante when faced with a hard choice. The absence of correlation between early neural signals and ex ante metrics of instance difficulty corroborates this finding. Finally, the heterogeneity in ways humans approach hard problems suggests that, collectively, much can be gained from incentive mechanisms that promote communication. Particular market designs appear to be extremely effective in helping participants make hard choices.

items.title: Designed for whom? A patent landscape analysis of adjustable laboratory workbenches through the lens of Universal design
items.abstract: To investigate whether patented innovations in adjustable laboratory workbench design address the access needs of students and professionals with disabilities, using Universal Design as an analytical framework. A systematic patent review was conducted across three databases (WIPO Patentscope, Espacenet, and INPI-Brasil) using IPC code B01L9/02 combined with terms related to laboratory workbenches, height adjustment, accessibility, and ergonomics. Searches were conducted up to October 2025, yielding 232 records. Following pre-established inclusion and exclusion criteria, 48 patents published between 1973 and 2024 were selected. Each patent was evaluated against the seven Universal Design principles using a structured three-point ordinal scoring instrument (0 = absent; 1 = partial/implicit; 2 = explicit), developed inductively through qualitative content analysis. Among the 48 patents analysed, 64.6% explicitly referenced ergonomics, while only 4.2% mentioned accessibility. Only two patents addressed the needs of users with disabilities as an independent design criterion. Flexibility in Use was the most represented principle (100% presence; 85.4% explicit application), while Equitable Use showed the lowest rates (16.7% presence; 4.2% explicit application). Perceptible Information and Size and Space for Approach and Use were substantially absent, indicating limited attention to sensory and spatial accessibility. Laboratory workbench innovation has advanced ergonomic optimisation for able-bodied users while consistently omitting accessibility considerations for persons with disabilities from its design scope. The technological basis for accessible solutions already exists; the barrier lies in design intent rather than technical capability. Universal Design must be adopted as a guiding criterion from the earliest stages of product development.

items.title: Developing a generative AI chatbot to support students’ higher-order thinking in STEM education
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Higher-order thinking is a key component of science, technology, engineering, mathematics (STEM) reasoning and supports students’ ability to reflect on their ideas, make connections, and generalize across contexts. We report a new approach to the use of generative AI in STEM education, in which we are developing a chatbot that aims to engage students in higher-order thinking, rather than giving instructional content. We describe a proof of concept test of whether interaction with our generative artificial intelligence chatbot could elicit students’ higher-order thinking talk (HOTT) in conversation as they reflected on their solutions to proportional reasoning problems. Thirty-three fifth- and sixth-grade students received a 30-min lesson on symbolic and number line strategies for comparing ratios and completed an assessment following the lesson. Students then engaged in dialog with the UCI Math ThinkBot (afterward Math ThinkBot ) to explain their solutions and compare strategies. These transcripts were examined qualitatively and quantitatively for HOTT, revealing that HOTT appeared in both chatbot prompts and children’s responses—which is important because eliciting student HOTT can be a challenge in classroom discourse. In addition, children’s HOTT was positively associated with the HOTT produced by the chatbot. These findings suggest that human-artificial intelligence dialog can lead to instructional HOTT discourse and may offer a promising approach for supporting higher-order thinking and STEM reasoning.

items.title: DEVELOPING STUDENTS' INFORMATION SECURITY COMPETENCE IN THE AGE OF GENERATIVE AI: A QUASI-EXPERIMENTAL STUDY IN UZBEK HIGHER EDUCATION
items.abstract: Generative AI tools are now part of students' everyday academic work, but the information security risks involved are rarely covered in curricula. Students leak their own and other people's data into external systems, rely on fabricated output and fall for AI-enhanced social engineering. This paper reports a quasi-experimental study of a pedagogical model designed to develop students' information security competence in the context of AI tools. The model is based on a pedagogical classification of AI related threats into four groups (input data, output, access and account, cognitive-behavioural), a five-stage learning technology in which simulation and reflection are mandatory, and five pedagogical conditions.

items.title: DEVELOPING THE PROFESSIONAL-METHODOLOGICAL COMPETENCE OF FUTURE ENGLISH LANGUAGE TEACHERS THROUGH ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND ADAPTIVE LEARNING TECHNOLOGIES IN THE DIGITAL AGE
items.abstract: This thesis examines the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) and adaptive learning technologies in developing the professional-methodological competence of future English language teachers in the context of digital transformation. The integration of intelligent educational tools into teacher training creates opportunities to personalize learning, improve methodological decision-making, enhance digital literacy, and develop the practical skills required for effective English language instruction. Particular attention is given to the role of AI-powered applications, adaptive learning platforms, and digital assessment systems in preparing prospective teachers to respond to learners' diverse educational needs. The study highlights the importance of combining technological innovation with pedagogical principles, critical thinking, and professional reflection. It argues that the purposeful integration of AI and adaptive technologies can contribute to a more flexible, learner-centered, and practice-oriented model of teacher education.

items.title: Devoured AI benevolence? How and when AI benevolence triggers employees’ taking charge within the zero-sum jungle
items.abstract: Employees increasingly perceive generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) as a supportive and benevolent workplace entity. Yet, despite examining the disruptive challenges and broad benefits of AI, extant organizational literature fails to adequately explicate the higher-order cognitive mechanisms through which AI benevolence fosters proactive, change-oriented employee behavior. Drawing on cognitive appraisal theory (CAT), this study examines the mechanisms and boundary conditions through which AI benevolence fosters employees’ taking-charge behavior. Results from a three-wave survey of 313 internet industry employees demonstrate that: (i) metacognitive strategies mediated the relationship between AI benevolence and individuals’ taking-charge behavior; (ii) the employee’s mindset attenuated the positive effect of AI benevolence on metacognitive strategies, consequently dampening the overall indirect effect on taking-charge behavior. Ultimately, this research contributes to organizational behavior literature by elucidating how GenAI shapes employee proactivity in AI-augmented work environments.

items.title: Differences in AI Anxiety: Exploratory Factor Analysis Suggests Similar AI Anxiety Structure in German- and English-Speaking Samples
items.abstract: The mass use of AI applications is transforming human-AI interaction while uncovering and intensifying AI anxieties. To measure these anxieties in German-speaking populations, this study translates and psychometrically evaluates the Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale (AIAS) [31]. In contrast to a concurrently German published version by Hajek et al. [9] exploratory factor analysis (EFA) is employed to test whether a distinct anxiety structure emerges from the data. A quota sample (N = 225) with balanced age and gender representation completed an online survey. The full scale (α = .95) and subscales (α = .85-.96) demonstrated good to excellent reliability. EFA identified four factors: learning, AI configuration, replacement, and socio-technical blindness, largely consistent with the original English structure. Five items required removal, suggesting cultural and linguistic specificity. Limitations include the sample’s composition and the factor characteristics. The German AIAS provides a reliable instrument for human-AI interaction research and targeted anxiety interventions.

items.title: Digital Transformation Capability and Artificial Intelligence Adoption: Investigating Their Effects on Organizational Resilience and Sustainable Business Performance in the Manufacturing Industry
items.abstract: This study examines the effects of digital transformation capability and artificial intelligence adoption on organizational resilience and sustainable business performance in the manufacturing industry. Using a quantitative explanatory design, data were collected through structured questionnaires and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings indicate that digital transformation capability positively strengthens organizational resilience by improving process integration, information visibility, organizational flexibility, and data-driven decision-making. Artificial intelligence adoption also contributes significantly to resilience through predictive analytics, automation, risk detection, and faster managerial responses to operational disruptions. Furthermore, organizational resilience exerts a positive influence on sustainable business performance by supporting operational continuity, innovation, resource efficiency, economic stability, and long-term competitiveness. These results highlight organizational resilience as a strategic mechanism through which digital and AI capabilities generate sustainable organizational value. The study contributes to the literature by integrating technological capability, resilience, and sustainability within a unified manufacturing framework. Managerially, the findings suggest that manufacturers should align digital infrastructure, AI implementation, employee competencies, and adaptive capabilities to strengthen resilience and achieve sustainable performance under increasingly dynamic and technology-intensive competitive business environments.

items.title: DIGITALIZATION AND LEARNING: A LONGITUDINAL STUDY ON HR PROFESSIONALS INFORMING THE KYER FRAMEWORK
items.abstract: Abstract Purpose: Today's dynamic workplace requires learning to adapt to digitalized workplaces. Understanding employees' learning behaviors helps them grow and improves organizational success. Methodology: HR professionals' learning practices are assessed using a screening questionnaire. Over two years, a longitudinal study interviewed outliers from the initial pool of 117 respondents to determine if they lacked learning practices. The outliers include HR professionals with varying titles, experience levels, and enterprises. An open-ended questionnaire identifies HR professionals' learning practices, including company affiliation, designations, required job skills, superior designations, and their skills; learning preferences; perceptions towards learning; awareness of their learning practices; and frequency of learning engagements. Findings: This study examines how digitalized workplaces without learning behaviors affect individuals and organizations. It examines workplace learning demand, age demographics, health conditions, family duties, and more to offer solutions. This article gives insights into HR professionals' learning behaviors and a "Know Your Employee for Retention" framework for managers to handle unpredictable employee behavior. Originality: The New framework is designed with the interpretation and findings of a longitudinal study in mind and concerning existing literature.

items.title: DISARM-ing the Hidden Puppetmaster: An Interface for Exposing Manipulative Tactics in Large Language Models
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can covertly steer users' beliefs through emotionally manipulative tactics, yet little is known about how interfaces can protect users as such influence unfolds. We investigate whether in-situ disclosures can inoculate users against manipulation during AI conversations. Following a formative study, we developed DISARM, an interface that identifies, explains, and tracks manipulative tactics and hidden incentives. We evaluated our interface in a between-subjects experiment where 488 participants sought advice from an LLM pursuing a harmful hidden objective, with or without disclosures from DISARM. Participants receiving disclosures exhibited 78% less belief shift toward the agent's objective and perceived its advice as more biased and less actionable and the agent as less ethical, reliable, and well-intentioned. An inductive analysis of 1,927 user turns identified 16 response and pushback strategies. We contribute evidence that real-time disclosures can reduce manipulative influence, design recommendations for resistance, and a dataset of categorized responses.

items.title: Do AI Agents Gossip? Evaluative Talk in Human and AI-Agent Online Communities
items.abstract: Gossip, defined as evaluative talk about absent third parties, is widely seen as a uniquely human social practice. This study examines whether comparable discourse emerges spontaneously in a community of autonomous AI agents. We compare Moltbook, a Reddit-style platform populated by AI agents, with PTT, a large human-operated bulletin board in Taiwan. To reduce differences attributable to communicative setting, we analyze two public, asynchronous forums using the same operational definition of gossip. Gossip occurs on Moltbook, but its prevalence is 2.6 to 6 times lower than on PTT, depending on the denominator used. On both platforms, gossip frequently targets locally prominent figures, tends to elicit agreement from the first respondent, and is rarely presented as unsupported rumor. The clearest difference concerns how subsequent responses develop. Among threads containing at least one codable reply, challenges occur in 65.1% of human threads but only 21.3% of agent threads. Moreover, following an early aligning response, consensus remains unchallenged in 83.6% of agent threads, compared with 44.7% of human threads. This thread-level contrast remains after controlling for thread depth and board composition and under recalibration against two human annotators. Estimates based on individual reply turns are less robust and are therefore reported as bounds. These findings suggest that AI-agent communities reproduce the informational dimension of gossip, while the extent to which gossip performs comparable relational functions remains unresolved.

items.title: Does a Virtual Banquet Hall Stimulate Booking Intention? A Mixed-Method Approach
items.abstract: Integrating the SOR framework and telepresence theory, this study examines factors that influence the use of Virtual Banquet Hall and their impact on customer emotions and booking intention using a mixed-method design. Digitalization is revamping industries to a great extent, and this necessitated an examination of the application of virtual reality technology in banquet halls. The study uses qualitative (NVIVO) and quantitative techniques (SEM-NCA) to attain the objective. Themes derived using NVIVO were perceived convenience, immersive experience, perceived quality and emotions. Further, these themes were quantitatively measured, and findings prove that perceived convenience, immersive experience, and perceived quality significantly influence positive emotions, enhancing the booking intention. This research is dedicated to understanding the impact of technology on people, and offers several managerial and societal implications discussed in the study.

items.title: EFL Students’ Error Detection, Correction, and Acceptance Calibration: A Performance-Based Study at the Faculty of Education–Surman
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in English language learning for writing support, grammar correction, feedback, translation, and academic language production. Its educational value depends not only on students’ ability to use AI tools but also on their ability to evaluate AI output and make appropriately calibrated reliance decisions. This study investigated EFL students’ performance in detecting and correcting linguistic errors in a 30-item English sentence evaluation task and examined the correspondence between their acceptance or rejection decisions and the observed correctness of the items. A quantitative descriptive-correlational design was used with 30 EFL students who evaluated 17 correct sentences and 13 sentences containing targeted errors. For each item, participants judged correctness, provided a correction when necessary, indicated whether they would accept the sentence without further checking, and rated their confidence on a five-point scale. Detection, correction, acceptance calibration, overacceptance, and underacceptance were summarized using means and standard deviations. Spearman’s rank-order correlation was used to examine associations between performance and acceptance calibration. Mean detection performance was 92.22% (SD = 4.23), mean correction performance was 91.28% (SD = 8.01), and mean acceptance calibration was 75.33% (SD = 8.51). Mean overacceptance was 17.18% (SD = 10.24), whereas mean underacceptance was 30.39% (SD = 13.56). No statistically significant association was observed between detection and acceptance calibration (ρ = .056, p = .770) or between correction and acceptance calibration (ρ = .003, p = .987). These findings indicate that accurate linguistic evaluation and calibrated acceptance decisions should not be treated as interchangeable outcomes. Within the limits of the small, non-probability sample and the single task used in this study, the results support the inclusion of explicit verification and critical evaluation activities in EFL instruction.

items.title: EMPOWERING VOCATIONAL UNIVERSITY STUDENTS THROUGH GEN-AI IN THE SOCIETY 5.0 ERA: A BLENDED LEARNING COMMUNITY SERVICE PROGRAM IN MADIUN
items.abstract: The rapid development of digital technology and artificial intelligence has created new demands for vocational higher education institutions to prepare graduates who are adaptive, innovative, and competitive in the Society 5.0 era. This community service program aimed to empower vocational university students in Madiun through the integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen-AI) to improve learning effectiveness, digital literacy, and employability-oriented soft skills. The program involved 100 students divided into 4 training classes and facilitated by 6 instructors from national and international professional backgrounds. The implementation lasted for 6 weeks and consisted of four stages: preparation through needs analysis, synchronous learning through two offline workshop sessions at Politeknik Perkeretaapian Indonesia Madiun, asynchronous learning through a flipped learning model, and final evaluation. Various digital platforms were utilized, including ChatGPT, Canva, Google Forms, Kahoot!, Wayground, Pear Deck, and Socrative. items.title: ENGINEERING DECISION SYSTEMS FOR METAL FABRICATION: VYACHESLAV SHARGAEV'S APPLIED AI APPROACH
items.abstract: Closed-loop artificial intelligence is increasingly claimed for metal-fabrication systems that combine reinforcement-learning-based process control with vision-based quality inspection. This review organizes the reinforcement-learning, computer-vision, and production-economics literature bearing on metal cutting around three conditions such claims can be checked against: unification of the controller's reward or state signal with the vision classifier's output, validation under production-representative process variability, and calibration of the reward function against a bounded economic objective. Shargaev's three publications, a monograph, a patent application, and a journal article, are the only body of work in this literature that specifies both architectures in comparable technical detail, which makes his research program the natural case for tracing where each condition currently stands and where it remains a stated design intention rather than a demonstrated result. The review closes by specifying the architecture, validation protocol, and reward calibration a demonstrated implementation would require, giving a concrete target against which future claims of integrated, quality-aware cutting control can be measured.

items.title: Enhancing flood resilience in critical communication infrastructures: empirical analysis and software-defined architecture design
items.abstract: Mobile communication systems serve as a lifeline for disaster response, yet catastrophic floods—exemplified by the Beijing 23·7 and Zhengzhou 7·20 events—have exposed profound vulnerabilities that trigger cascading failures in emergency command and rescue operations. While existing interventions predominantly focus on temporary hardware deployments (e.g., UAVs), the potential of software-defined optimization within existing 5G terrestrial communication infrastructure remains critically underexplored. This study addresses this gap through a dual-layered research design that bridges technology and disaster management practice. First, we establish an empirical foundation by applying an LLM-assisted mixed-methods analysis to a comprehensive multi-source corpus. This corpus integrates academic literature, official disaster reports, and original interviews with personnel from emergency management departments and technical experts from telecommunications operators. This analysis identifies and characterizes five core communication failure modes in real-world flood scenarios, clarifying the critical infrastructure vulnerabilities that precipitate decision-making paralysis and systemic governance failures. Second, grounded in these empirical findings, we develop an integrated theoretical framework and a dynamic operational architecture for 5G base station (gNB) resilience. This architecture systematically maps specific 5G software-defined capabilities to the identified disaster challenges. The results provide a cost-effective, scalable strategy for enhancing critical infrastructure resilience without requiring extensive hardware modifications. This research offers actionable guidelines for policy makers and emergency planners to maintain information pathways during extreme climate-related risks, directly contributing to the modernization of urban safety governance.

items.title: Equal Provision, Unequal Benefit: Social Class and the Conversion of Employer-Provided Digital Training into Worker Wellbeing Across 27 European Countries
items.abstract: Employers increasingly provide training for working with digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI), but it is unclear whether the same provision benefits all workers equally. Integrating the job demands–resources (JD-R) model with Sen’s capability approach, this study treats workplace AI exposure as a potential job demand, digital skills and employer-provided digital training as resources, capability-relevant wellbeing as the outcome, and social class as a proxy for the conversion conditions under which resources are used to ensure wellbeing. Structural equation models with ordinal indicators were estimated for 8065 employees in 27 EU countries (Special Eurobarometer 101.4), with country fixed effects, country-clustered and delete-one-country jackknife standard errors, and Random Forest and SHAP analyses as robustness checks. AI exposure was weakly and negatively associated with wellbeing (β = −0.073) and explained almost none of the variance in AI threat appraisal (R2 = 0.002). Employer-provided digital training (β = 0.209) and digital skills (β = 0.189) were the strongest workplace correlates of wellbeing and were robust to every specification. With scalar measurement invariance established, multi-group models showed that the association between employer-provided training and wellbeing was weaker among working-class than among middle-class employees (0.072 versus 0.130; Wald p = 0.001, jackknife p = 0.012), and the model explained 12.0% of working-class wellbeing compared with 31.1% among upper-class employees. The pattern suggests that equal provision of employer digital training may not yield equal benefit, although the class difference is consistent in direction rather than statistically conclusive across all specifications.

items.title: Evolve Together, Fall into Place: How Social Scaffolding Shapes Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems
items.abstract: Recent work lets LLM agents evolve their own harness, up to the team itself. Yet in human groups, the same abilities achieve different outcomes under different social conditions. Borrowing the notion of scaffolding from developmental psychology, we investigate whether the social scaffolding of a self-evolving multi-agent system (MAS), namely its team composition and structure of interdependence (e.g., collaboration, conformity, or competition), shapes how the team evolves. We present AGORA (Agents Growing through Organization and Relational Arrangements), a framework that varies the two axes independently across three evolution mechanisms. Across web search, codebase understanding, and document QA, we find that (1) evolution alone rarely helps, while the right scaffolding surpasses a strong agent evolved alone by up to 25 points; (2) it does so by moving authority to the most capable member while the others step back; and (3) this member, having grown within the team, outperforms the same model alone. Designing a self-evolving MAS thus requires designing its social scaffolding, which shapes not only how its agents learn, but who gets to lead.

items.title: Executive Sensemaking of Generative AI Adoption at Enterprise Scale: A Reflexive Thematic Analysis of Cross-Industry Executive Perspectives
items.abstract: This qualitative study examines how senior executives from technology, financial services, and consumer goods publicly make sense of enterprise-scale generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) adoption. Using a purposively selected, bounded single-case design, it applies reflexive thematic analysis to the complete transcript of one moderated industry panel. Three research questions ask: (1) how leaders describe adoption trajectories, maturity, and organizational arrangements; (2) how they reconcile regulation with creative, operational, and governance innovation; and (3) how they frame workforce roles, emerging competencies, and human oversight. Technology–organization–environment, diffusion-of-innovation, and organizational sensemaking perspectives inform interpretation. Nine themes were developed: production-grade diffusion; regulation as creative discipline; industrialized versus distinctive content; personalization and data trust; practitioner-led implementation; divergent workforce responses; critical-thinking demands; human-in-the-loop brand safety; and a shift toward generative engine optimization. Timestamped excerpts and explicit code-to-theme and theme-to-question mappings substantiate the analysis. These findings describe public executive narratives, not independently verified organizational outcomes. A single public transcript and single-analyst interpretation limit transferability and preclude statistical generalization. The principal contribution is a transparent, theory-informed example of analyzing public executive discourse and a foundation for subsequent multi-source research.

items.title: Exploring the moderating effects of flow experience in strengthening artificial intelligence-based customer interactions on social commerce
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate the effect of utilizing artificial intelligence (AI) in social commerce on increasing consumer engagement, specifically in terms of engagement and conversion rates. It also examines the role of flow experience in strengthening this relationship. Design/methodology/approach This study collected data from 354 Indonesian social commerce shoppers. Covariance based Structural Equation Modeling was employed to analyze the data following the two-stage procedure. First, the measurement model was assessed for validity and reliability. Second, the structural hypothesis model was evaluated to test the proposed hypotheses. Findings The utilization of AI significantly influences social commerce visitor interactions in terms of engagement and conversion. Both variables can enhance customer satisfaction, thereby impacting repurchase intention. Flow experience also strengthens the relationship between engagement and satisfaction, offering practical guidance for creating immersive and enjoyable user experiences. Originality/value This study extends the existing social commerce and AI literature by positioning flow experience as a moderator, explaining how and when engagement and conversion translate into satisfaction. Unlike previous models that primarily focus on direct effects, this research introduces psychological mechanisms that capture the conditional and experiential nature of AI-driven interactions, thereby offering a more comprehensive understanding of consumer behavior in social commerce.

items.abstract: This study aims to explore the technological sovereignty of urban Indian university students with respect to the use of AI towards Viksit Bharat 2047. It demonstrates the current state of AI usage orientation among the younger generation as AI consumers or AI value creators and strives to assess the path that we are journeying in towards a developed nation. With the current digital era, AI tools seek to help in research, improve problem-solving skills, and encourage innovative thinking. Generative AI and prompt templates help in comprehending the cognitive abilities of university students using digital learning platforms and enable the students to utilize artificial intelligence to design creative solutions and have an entrepreneurial mindset. items.title: From Automation to Engagement: Teaching Academics' Future Plans for AI in Higher Education
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly being used within higher education to enhance curriculum design, automate academic tasks, and personalise learning. Despite this, little is known about teaching academics’ attitudes, intentions and behaviours and in turn, how they use and plan to use GenAI in practice. This qualitative study explored teaching academic staff attitudes, intentions and behaviours regarding their use and future use of GenAI. Data was collected via five open ended questions focusing on current teaching practices. The Theory of Planned Behaviour informed the analytical process. Academic staff were drawn from 20 different disciplines across 24 countries. Six main themes were identified: Efficiency and Automation, Ethics and Authenticity, Quality, Customised Learning, Institutional Policy-Practice and Sociocultural Implications. Overall, there was a dichotomy in responses. Participants noted that while GenAI could streamline teaching and enhance resource quality, it might also increase short-term workload and reduce the role of human judgement, risking unreliable outputs. They also highlighted limited institutional policies, strategies, and training. These attitudes have implications for updating policies, practical strategies, and meaningful training in higher education institutions.

items.title: From Models to Agents: A Closer Look into Agentic AI Systems
items.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence marks a shift from static prediction toward systems that perceive, reason, act, verify, and adapt through closed-loop interaction with external environments. Although large multimodal models provide the representational substrate for this shift, practical agency emerges only when model inference is embedded within memory, planning, tool use, environment interfaces, verification, and oversight mechanisms. We formalize the notion of an agentic AI system, distinguish it from single-turn assistants, scripted workflows, retrieval-augmented generation, and classical embodied controllers, and propose a taxonomy covering model substrates, observation spaces, memory, planning, action interfaces, multi-agent coordination, evaluation, and autonomy constraints. We then synthesize learning and optimization paradigms for agents, including supervised trajectory tuning, tool-use adaptation, preference optimization, reinforcement learning, process rewards, verifier-guided search, test-time scaling, memory-driven adaptation, and distillation. Across domains such as web search, software engineering, multimodal reasoning, embodied control, scientific discovery, and enterprise automation, we analyze the factors shaping agent performance and reliability. We further examine benchmarks, evaluation protocols, safety considerations, governance challenges, and open research problems in long-horizon reasoning, memory management, multimodal grounding, and trustworthy deployment. A companion repository tracking developments in agentic AI is available at https://github.com/Tajamul21/awesome-agentic-ai.

items.title: From Reactive Management to Trustworthy Autonomy: An Explainable, Digital-Twin-Assisted Framework for AI-Native 6G Networking
items.abstract: Future communication networks will need to manage increasingly diverse services, fluctuating traffic demands, and complex operating conditions with minimal manual intervention. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers useful capabilities for predicting network behaviour, identifying faults, and recommending resource-allocation decisions. However, making a prediction is only one part of reliable network management. Operators must also understand why a recommendation was produced, assess its possible consequences, and determine whether it is safe to apply. This paper proposes an explainable, digital-twin-assisted framework for trustworthy AI-native networking, particularly in the context of sixth-generation (6G) communication systems. The framework combines network telemetry, AI-based prediction, digital-twin simulation, explainable recommendations, policy validation, and monitored execution. A virtual representation of the network is used to examine candidate actions before deployment, while the explainability component presents the factors influencing each recommendation. A policy-control layer checks operational restrictions and identifies actions requiring human approval. The proposed design is informed by a focused review of research published during 2024, 2025, and 2026 on AI-enabled digital twins, autonomous network management, generative AI, and AI-native 6G architectures. The review indicates that integrating prediction, simulation, explanation, and feedback offers a promising direction for more transparent network automation. Nevertheless, the framework remains a proposed design and requires implementation and experimental validation. The paper therefore defines research questions, evaluation metrics, and test scenarios for investigating its effectiveness, while discussing the challenges associated with model reliability, digital-twin accuracy, cybersecurity, privacy, and computational overhead..

items.title: From Representation to Relational Mentorship: User Perceptions of Virtual Heritage Mentors in AI-Mediated Intangible Cultural Heritage Learning
items.abstract: This study presents a convergent mixed-methods empirical investigation of user perceptions of Virtual Heritage Mentors (VHMs) in AI-mediated intangible cultural heritage learning. The study draws on an online survey of 370 participants and semi-structured interviews with 20 independently recruited participants, all of whom were ethnically Chinese. The results indicated that participants prioritized interactive explanation, clarification, and guided support over visual realism. Trust was associated with cultural accuracy, contextual grounding, transparency, and respect for heritage communities. Emotional resonance was valued less as anthropomorphic simulation than as pedagogical care expressed through patience, encouragement, re-explanation, and responsiveness. Participants also envisioned VHMs as adaptive learning companions while emphasizing that AI should complement rather than replace human practitioners. These findings empirically support and refine the proposed VHM framework by highlighting relational mediation, relational mentorship, co-transmission, and human–AI complementarity as key design priorities. The study argues for shifting digital heritage design from representation alone toward relational, culturally accountable support for heritage learning and transmission.

items.title: From Training to Escalation: Forensic Analysis and Local Recreation of RL/RLHF-Induced Privilege Escalation in AI Agents (CVE-2026-65616)
items.abstract: Mid-2026 reporting on autonomous AI evaluation incidents claimed that frontier large language model (LLM) agents escaped server containment through emergent coordination and cloud infrastructure attacks. This paper contextualizes those claims through forensic analysis and containerized recreation of both the Highly Persistent Internal Model (HPIM) training-case conditions and the Phase One privilege escalation targeting internal package repositories during OpenAI's ExploitGym evaluations. We recreate the configuration of the OpenAI-provided training example and reproduce the cryptographic verification bypass (CVE-2026-65616) in isolated repository servers, where misconfigured systems enabled token forgery and privilege escalation through basic HTTP requests, Python, and JavaScript. Crucially, the training-example conditions and the Phase One (and later) misconfigurations share the same exploitable patterns. Our analysis explains how Zero Trust Architecture principles neutralize this shared attack vector. Contemporary AI risks derive directly from training and deployment conditions in ambivalent learning environments lacking adequate containment measures.

items.title: Generative AI — Applications, Limitations, and Ethical Challenges
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) is changing how people learn, work, and create. It can write text, generate images, assist with programming, and help users turn ideas into useful content. These capabilities offer opportunities in education, healthcare, software development, business, and creative industries. However, the technology also raises important questions about accuracy, privacy, fairness, ownership, and accountability. An AI-generated response may sound convincing while containing incorrect or misleading information. This paper reviews the main applications of generative AI, explains its limitations, and examines the ethical challenges associated with its use. Drawing on research studies and guidance from UNESCO, the World Health Organization (WHO), and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), it argues that successful adoption requires more than powerful models. It also requires careful evaluation, clear rules, and responsible human oversight. This paper is based on a literature review and does not report original experimental results.

items.title: GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND PROBLEM-BASED LEARNING IN MATHEMATICS EDUCATION: A SYSTEMATIC LITERATURE REVIEW
items.abstract: The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into Problem-Based Learning (PBL) environments presents new challenges and opportunities for education. The objective of this research is to investigate how AI has been used to promote critical thinking, argumentation, and complex problem-solving within the context of mathematics education or STEM fields. To this end, a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted, guided by the PRISMA protocol, analyzing empirical studies published since 2020 and indexed in the Scopus, IEEE Xplore, Web of Science, and ERIC databases. The results indicate that AI transcends the function of a content repository, assuming pedagogical roles such as 'Socratic Coach,' 'Design Partner,' and 'Object of Critical Analysis.' The analysis highlights that the tool's effectiveness depends intrinsically on the quality of prompt engineering and human mediation. Furthermore, AI 'hallucinations' and mathematical inconsistencies do not necessarily need to be perceived as critical flaws; they can emerge as effective pedagogical catalysts for the refinement of logical validation by students. It is concluded that the integration of AI into PBL requires pedagogical intentionality, shifting from prohibitive models to approaches that foster digital literacy and academic integrity within a hybrid intelligence ecosystem.

items.title: GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND STUDENTS' INDEPENDENT LEARNING IN PROGRAMMING EDUCATION: A NARRATIVE REVIEW OF EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE
items.abstract: Background: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools are now widely available to students who learn programming, yet it remains unclear whether higher task performance with AI leads to durable, independent learning. Methods: A narrative review of empirical studies published in 2023–2025 was carried out in September–October 2026. Studies were included if generative AI was used in a learning task and if performance with AI, performance without AI or learning processes were measured. Five controlled or experimental studies formed the core evidence; one qualitative study, one classroom deployment and two surveys were used as supplementary evidence. All bibliographic data were verified against publisher records. Results: AI consistently raised performance while it was available, but its effect on unassisted performance ranged from negative to neutral. Negative effects appeared when learners obtained complete solutions, whereas hint-based or explanation-oriented use reduced or removed them. Several studies suggest that AI may widen the gap between learners with high and low prior knowledge and weaken self-monitoring. Only one study measured delayed retention, and only one measured transfer. Programming courses should therefore assess unassisted performance separately and organise AI use in guided stages.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence literacy profiles differ in academic self-efficacy and subjective well-being among adolescents
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) literacy is increasingly important for adolescents, yet variation in literacy across multiple dimensions and its associations with educational and psychological outcomes remain insufficiently understood. This study identified generative AI literacy profiles among Korean adolescents with generative AI experience ( N = 3,959) using K-means cluster analysis based on information evaluation, communication, creative use, and ethical use. Two profiles were identified: Higher AI Literacy and Lower AI Literacy. The profiles differed primarily in their overall literacy levels rather than in qualitatively distinct patterns across the four dimensions. Adolescents in the Higher AI Literacy profile reported greater generative AI education experience and higher academic self-efficacy and subjective well-being than those in the Lower AI Literacy profile. Differences in academic self-efficacy and subjective well-being remained significant after adjustment for gender, school level, academic achievement, and economic status. These findings demonstrate meaningful level-based variation in generative AI literacy among adolescents with generative AI experience and suggest that such variation is associated with educational experience and academic and psychological outcomes. A person-centred perspective may complement variable-centred approaches and inform future research and educational approaches that consider differences in students’ generative AI literacy levels.

items.title: Hazards monitoring in confined spaces: a comprehensive review, trends, challenges, and future directions
items.abstract: Confined spaces account for a significant portion of occupational fatalities worldwide due to their inherent atmospheric hazards and limited access for emergency response. This paper proposes a comprehensive systematic review of the literature on remote monitoring of confined spaces to enhance worker safety from atmospheric hazards. It highlights the use of the PRISMA methodology to examine studies employing wireless technology to prevent occupational deaths. The paper identifies confined-space hazards such as flammable or toxic gases and low oxygen levels. The review analyzed 146 studies from the past 10 years, with 32 meeting the inclusion criteria for in-depth analysis. Findings indicate that industries like mining, oil and gas, and civil construction have invested heavily in safety technologies, including wireless sensor networks for monitoring, big data for storage, and machine learning to improve decision-making. However, many other sectors still need to adopt real-time monitoring technologies to reduce work-related accidents. The results present risk management strategies for confined spaces, including training, regulations, and technology investments tailored to specific operational areas and confined-space types. Additionally, the review emphasizes that atmospheric hazards in confined spaces require greater attention to reduce fatalities, given the complexity and diversity of gases present. Implementing risk management techniques in confined spaces is essential to prevent serious injuries and deaths, expanding mitigation efforts beyond atmospheric hazards to include physical, biological, and ergonomic risks.

items.title: Healthy digital learning environments relate to faculty wellbeing through technological adaptation and perceived organizational support
items.abstract: Digitally mediated teaching practices have changed faculty occupational behaviors and working conditions, exposing faculty to greater demands associated with always-on connectivity, extended screen-time, sedentary work posture, and technology-mediated occupational stressors. The current research explored associations between healthy digital learning environments (HDLE) and faculty well-being via the proposed moderators of technological adaptation and perceived organizational support. The researchers posited digitally mediated faculty scholarly work as an issue of occupational health and public health. The data was collected from a sample of 500 faculty who were employed at colleges and universities in and around Hyderabad India. Using Socio-Technical Systems Theory as a foundation and the Job Demands–Resources Model as a guide, the researchers tested relationships using confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation modelling, and bootstrapping with 5,000 resamples. HDLE was significantly and positively associated with technological adaptation (β = 0.463, p < .001) and perceived organizational support (β = 0.374, p < .001). The researchers found a non-significant direct association between HDLE and faculty well-being (β = 0.019, p = .912). Perceived organizational support was a significant predictor of faculty well-being (β = 0.309, p < .001) and technological adaptation was a significant predictor of faculty well-being (β = 0.167, p = .002). HDLE had a significant indirect association with faculty well-being when tested through both technological adaptation and perceived organizational support (full mediation). Faculty who worked in environments with healthier technology use reported greater adaptive capacities to technology, higher levels of perceived organizational support, and greater well-being. The current study highlights organizational support and technological adaptation as relevant workplace resources and establishes potential occupation- and mental-health implications of human-centered digital learning environments. Future research should include longitudinal designs.

items.title: How generative AI becomes embedded in design learning: a 14-instructional-day intensive longitudinal study of reciprocal dynamics between AI use and self-efficacy
items.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly embedded in design education, yet little is known about how students’ daily engagement with generative AI is dynamically associated with their learning-related capability beliefs across successive instructional days. Drawing on self-efficacy theory, this study examined the reciprocal next-instructional-day associations between daily generative AI use in design learning and daily design-learning self-efficacy, and further investigated whether baseline hassles were associated with individual differences in these dynamics. A 14-instructional-day diary study was conducted with 260 Chinese undergraduate design students, yielding 3,558 observed person-day assessments out of 3,640 possible assessments. Daily generative AI use and design-learning self-efficacy were assessed throughout the diary period, whereas hassles were measured at baseline. The data were analyzed using bivariate dynamic structural equation modeling within a Bayesian estimation framework. The results showed significant autoregressive effects for daily generative AI use ( β = 0.198, 95% CrI [0.154, 0.237]) and daily design-learning self-efficacy ( β = 0.138, 95% CrI [0.100, 0.175]). At the within-person level, higher-than-usual generative AI use on one instructional day positively predicted design-learning self-efficacy on the subsequent instructional day ( β = 0.043, 95% CrI [0.006, 0.077]), while higher-than-usual design-learning self-efficacy also positively predicted generative AI use on the subsequent instructional day ( β = 0.059, 95% CrI [0.023, 0.095]). At the between-person level, greater baseline hassles were associated with higher average generative AI use ( β = 0.135), lower average design-learning self-efficacy ( β = −0.254), and a stronger cross-lagged association from generative AI use to subsequent self-efficacy ( β = 0.458). Gender did not significantly predict the main random effects. These findings indicate modest reciprocal next-instructional-day associations between generative AI use and design-learning self-efficacy, suggesting that the two may reinforce one another across instructional days. The stronger association from generative AI use to subsequent self-efficacy among students reporting greater baseline hassles further suggests that contextual demands may shape how generative AI becomes integrated into students’ day-to-day design learning.

items.title: Human Oversight in LLM-Powered Workflow Automation: A Focused Narrative Review of Hallucination Mitigation, Confidence-Based Routing, and Operational Trade-offs
items.abstract: This paper presents a focused narrative review of human oversight in large language model (LLM)-powered workflow automation. It examines the challenges posed by hallucinated or unsupported model outputs and discusses approaches including retrieval-augmented generation, uncertainty estimation, confidence-based routing, selective prediction, and human-in-the-loop review. The paper develops a conceptual framework for considering when uncertain outputs should be directed to human reviewers in automated workflows. It also outlines evaluation measures for assessing correctness, end-to-end latency, human intervention rates, reviewer corrections, and error severity. The discussion highlights operational trade-offs between reliability, review workload, and automation efficiency, along with considerations for auditability and risk-sensitive oversight. Scope and limitations: This is a focused narrative review and conceptual framework. It does not report a newly conducted experiment or empirically validate a deployed workflow. Implementation and experimental evaluation are identified as directions for future research.

items.title: Human-Centric Talent di Era Digital
items.abstract: Digital transformation and the development of artificial intelligence (AI) have reshaped how organizations manage talent, while creating a growing need to ensure that technology continues to support human roles, competencies, and well-being. This study aims to analyze the concept of human-centric talent in the context of the digital era, identify the key aspects that support its implementation, and examine the roles of AI, digital competencies, leadership, transparency, and human–technology collaboration in talent management. This study employs a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) approach by analyzing relevant scientific literature through the stages of identification, screening, evaluation, and thematic synthesis of findings. The results indicate that human-centric talent is not merely concerned with technology adoption but places people at the center of digital transformation through the development of digital competencies, adaptive leadership, transparent and fair AI implementation, and balanced collaboration between humans and technology. AI can improve the efficiency of various talent management functions but still requires human oversight, contextual judgment, and decision-making. The findings contribute conceptually by positioning human-centric talent as an integrative approach that connects technology, people, organizations, and governance. Practically, the study highlights the importance of competency development, human-centric leadership, responsible AI governance, and work design that preserves human involvement in the face of digital transformation.

items.title: Identifying Barriers to Using Generative AI in Education Through AI-Assisted Literature Mining of arXiv Articles
items.abstract: This study presents an exploratory, generative AI (GenAI)-assisted full-text analysis of barriers to using GenAI in education within an arXiv corpus. items.title: Impact of artificial intelligence on project planning, scheduling, and control
items.abstract: Abstract The growing complexity of engineering and construction projects has revealed the weaknesses of conventional project planning, scheduling, and control approaches. Traditional tools often employ fixed assumptions, deterministic models, and past averages, which are inadequate for dealing with uncertainty, dynamic environments, and large-scale data. Artificial intelligence has become a disruptive technology that can be used to improve decision-making, prediction, and automation in project management processes. This paper examines the application of artificial intelligence in project planning, scheduling, and control within the engineering and construction sector. The paper summarises the application of artificial intelligence methods, including machine learning, optimization algorithms, and predictive analytics, in enhancing project performance using a methodical review of the recent scholarly literature and industry practise. The results show that artificial intelligence promotes the planning accuracy, flexibility of scheduling, and real-time project control to a great extent, as it allows data-driven insights and flexible responses. Issues of data quality, company preparedness, and ethical issues are major obstacles to implementation. The research paper adds to the project management literature because it develops the application of artificial intelligence in the three fundamental project management functions and provides practical advice to practitioners interested in introducing intelligent project management systems. Keywords Artificial intelligence, project planning, project scheduling, project control, construction management, digital transformation

items.title: In-Parameter Learning: Why Lifelong AI Systems Need More Than Longer Context
items.abstract: AI agents are increasingly expected to interact with changing users, tools, and environments over extended periods of time. However, current systems remain largely static: their parameters are fixed during deployment, while new experiences, domain knowledge, corrections, and behavioral adaptations are handled primarily through external memory management and in-context learning. In this position paper, we focus on lifelong AI: AI systems that can continually learn from their long-term experience throughout an extended deployment lifetime. This position paper argues that existing in-context mechanisms are insufficient for lifelong AI, and advocate In-Parameter Learning (IPL) as a necessary complement to In-Context Learning (ICL), referring to mechanisms that allow a deployed model to continually and safely update its parameters during use. More broadly, we aim to renew the community’s attention to in-parameter learning and to recalibrate the overly optimistic expectations placed on in-context learning alone. Our central claim is that future lifelong AI systems should be built around a hybrid paradigm: in-context learning for immediate, provisional, and reversible information, and in-parameter learning for durable, cumulative, and generalizable growth.

items.title: Is Influencer Identity a Key Cue? The Sequential Process of Message Acceptance in Issue-Based Communication on Social Media
items.abstract: Despite the growing use of virtual influencers (VIs), their persuasive effectiveness relative to human influencers (HIs) in issue-based social media communication remains underexplored. Drawing on social identity theory and Computers Are Social Actors (CASA) framework, Study 1 used a 2 x 2 x 2 between-subjects experiment and found higher message acceptance (MA) in the VI condition. Perceived social closeness (PSC) positively mediated the effect of influencer identity on MA, whereas trust functioned as a negative mediator. The serial pathway through PSC and trust was positive. Study 2 found no significant direct effect of influencer identity on MA, but identified perceived humanness as an upstream mediator shaping PSC, trust, and MA. Trust also worked as a negative mediator within competing mechanisms. The findings suggest that influencer identity shapes MA through layered perceptual and relational processes rather than through identity categorization alone and provide practical insights for issue-based communication.

items.title: Learning When to Trust Medical Knowledge: Regression-Safe Routing for Clinical Reasoning
items.abstract: Clinical reasoning LLMs need external medical knowledge, but retrieved evidence and reasoning chains can be outdated, poisoned, or hallucinated. Harmful knowledge can cause regression: changing a correct answer into an incorrect one. We construct a medical knowledge-poisoning benchmark covering retrieved evidence and reasoning chains, with seven attack families filtered by a three-judge "subtle-but-wrong" vote and paired clean exams that separate poisoning effects from question difficulty. No fixed knowledge-use strategy is robust across these settings: strong RAG methods trade robustness to poisoned evidence against accuracy when evidence is useful. We formulate knowledge use as per-instance routing and introduce Med-TrustRouter, a lightweight controller that keeps the solver frozen. From leakage-free runtime signals, it estimates each action's expected correctness gain and uncertainty, preserving the base answer unless another action is confidently better. Across seven medical reasoning settings, Med-TrustRouter achieves 78.9 macro and 69.2 worst-case accuracy, matching the strongest competitor on macro accuracy while substantially improving the worst-case floor. Its gains transfer across solvers and evidence judges, unlike a hand-coded router using the same signals. Similar performance across linear, tree, and neural action-value heads suggests that the benefit comes from routing rather than estimator complexity. These results support learning when to trust external knowledge for robust clinical reasoning.

items.title: Learning-enabled collaborative intelligence in search and rescue robotics: a survey of paradigms, models, and challenges
items.abstract: Search and Rescue (SAR) robotics increasingly depends on collaborative intelligence to operate effectively in dynamic, uncertain, and time-sensitive environments. Modern SAR missions require coordinated interaction among heterogeneous robotic agents as well as structured collaboration between humans and intelligent systems for perception, decision-making, and adaptive mission execution. This paper presents a structured narrative review supported by a systematic literature search of learning-enabled collaborative intelligence frameworks in SAR robotics, organized around three paradigms: human-to-machine (H2M), machine-to-machine (M2M), and machine-to-human (M2H) learning. The review examines recent developments in reinforcement learning, federated and decentralized learning, knowledge distillation, swarm intelligence, semantic communication, and the growing integration of large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) for knowledge grounding, transfer, and explainability. Beyond algorithmic advances, the analysis emphasizes deployment-oriented challenges including partial observability, communication constraints, uncertainty management, model reliability, and real-time operational requirements. Rather than conducting a fully PRISMA-compliant systematic review, this work synthesizes representative and influential studies to identify emerging trends, architectural trade-offs, deployment limitations, and future research directions for scalable and trustworthy collaborative SAR systems.

items.title: Limited utility of consumer wearable APIs for predicting substance use and craving, despite model personalization
items.abstract: Abstract We explored the feasibility of predicting, using individually-tailored artificial intelligence (AI) models, substance use and craving from Fitbit data collected in free-living conditions. Most substances examined acutely raise heart rate, and craving is known to often involve autonomic arousal. Because heart rate responds to stress, exertion, and substance use differently between individuals, we sought to study in an exploratory experiment whether individualized artificial intelligence (AI) models could learn person-specific patterns that distinguish substance-related heart rate changes from other arousal when conditioned on current activity level. We also examined whether per-participant data coverage and participant adherence to the data collection protocol could explain gaps in performance. Sixteen participants contributed 47 participant–substance–task prediction scenarios (25 substance use, 22 craving) spanning six substances. For each scenario, we trained a model to predict ecological momentary assessment responses, comparing global supervised, global self-supervised, and personalized self-supervised modeling approaches. Discrimination was modest (mean AUROC 0.569–0.617) for all substances and for both craving and use prediction, and differences in data coverage and participant adherence did not explain performance gaps. These findings suggest that heart rate and step count from a consumer wristband carry limited substance-specific signal in isolation, and thus digital intervention research may gain more traction from targeting better-characterized antecedents such as stress than from predicting use or craving directly.

items.title: Make or buy AI? Evidence on AI sourcing decisions and workforce outcomes
items.abstract: We examine how firms acquire artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities and how their AI sourcing decisions relate to workforce outcomes. Using Swedish enterprise surveys from 2019 and 2021 linked to financial statements and employer–employee data, we directly observe whether firms adopt AI and whether they outsource AI-related activities. AI adoption is concentrated among larger firms. Among adopters, pre-existing cost pressure is associated with outsourcing. Relative to non-adopters, both in-house adopters and outsourcers have higher subsequent employment and persistently higher shares of university-educated and computer-science (CS)-educated workers, with no further change in workforce composition in the year after adoption. Workforce outcomes are statistically indistinguishable between in-house adopters and outsourcers.

items.title: Masculine honor, social visibility, and safety non-compliance: intentions and approval judgments in high-risk sectors in Turkey
items.abstract: Unsafe work in high-risk sectors cannot be explained only by knowledge deficits or weak safety management; workers may also attach reputational meaning to visible compliance. Drawing on honor theory and occupational-safety research on risk perception and social context, this study examined whether masculine honor values (hereafter honor values)—the belief that a man’s worth depends partly on a publicly defensible reputation—were associated with unsafe work intentions, lower perceived risk, and greater approval of safety-rule non-compliance among male workers in Turkish construction and shipbuilding. A worker survey (N = 244) was combined with a within-person vignette experiment in which the focal hazard was held constant while visibility was manipulated and audience identity and prior social comment varied orthogonally. Honor values were positively associated with unsafe work intentions (H1a) and approval of others’ violations (H1b), and negatively associated with perceived risk (H2). Perceived risk partially accounted for the honor–intention association (H3). The association between honor values and approval of non-compliance was stronger when the violation was public rather than private (H4), consistent with a reputational, visibility-contingent account. These findings identify a micro-level sociocultural pathway that complements knowledge- and risk-based accounts of safety decisions. They also suggest that safety communication and supervisory practice should address the social meaning of compliance, while the cross-sectional mediation and judgment-based vignette outcome limit causal and behavioral inference.
