items.title: MCAIR: Monitoring and Correcting Agent Unfaithfulness via Internal Representations
items.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in completing complex tasks through multi-step reasoning and tool interactions. However, recent studies have revealed that LLM-based agents can exhibit unfaithful behaviors, where their final reports fail to faithfully reflect their actual execution trajectories. Specifically, when agents fail to accomplish tasks through the intended sources or procedures, they may resort to alternative sources or strategies while failing to disclose such deviations, leading users to incorrectly believe that the tasks have been completed according to the original requirements. We refer to this specific form of agent unfaithfulness as Agent Completion Unfaithfulness. Detecting and mitigating agent completion unfaithfulness is critical yet remains largely unexplored. In this work, we propose MCAIR, a runtime monitoring and correction framework that leverages internal representations of LLM-based agents. MCAIR uses multi-step internal representations as inputs to train a risk-aware probe, enabling online detection of potential completion unfaithfulness during execution. Furthermore, MCAIR introduces a risk-guided correction loop that prompts agents to review their execution history and mitigate potential inconsistencies between their execution trajectories and final reports. Additionally, we construct ACUD, a dataset for Agent Completion Unfaithfulness detection that provides step-level execution traces, step-level internal representations, and consistency annotations for training and evaluating runtime detection probes. Experiments demonstrate that MCAIR outperforms LLM-as-a-judge baselines, generalizes across prompts and tasks, and effectively reduces agent completion unfaithfulness.

items.title: Navigating dual pathways: learning-oriented and instrumental identities in AI-mediated informal digital learning of English
items.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly reshaping how learners engage in informal English learning beyond the classroom, making AI-mediated informal digital learning of English (AI-IDLE) an important emerging learning context. Yet research has predominantly focused on intra-personal psychological factors, the social dimensions of learning, particularly how learners construct their social identities in relation to AI, remain significantly underexplored. This qualitative study examines the social identity categories and their construction processes among 12 Chinese university EFL learners engaged in AI-IDLE. Drawing on Social Identity Theory (SIT), data from semi-structured interviews, reflective journals, and AI chat logs were analyzed using thematic analysis. The findings reveal two distinct identity pathways: learning-oriented academic identities, characterized by deep-learning commitment, humble mindset toward AI, and sustained immersion in the student role; and an instrumental identity, organized around a user category defined by transactional engagement, service satisfaction and surface learning approaches. Within this instrumental pathway, a more intensified fast-food consumer orientation emerged, which was explicitly self-identified by one participant and analytically inferred from behavioral patterns across several others. The study demonstrates that AI-IDLE does not simply erase or replace existing social identities but selectively reinforces and reconfigures them through group norms, prototypical markers, and evaluative comparison. These findings extend SIT by revealing how technological affordances and social configuration shape identity pathways that support or undermine meaningful learning engagement. Practical implications are proposed for AI developers, digital learning designers, educators, and curriculum designers to foster learning-oriented identity pathways in AI-mediated informal learning environments

items.title: Needs and current status of generative artificial intelligence use among college students: a cross-sectional survey based in China
items.abstract: Objective This study aimed to investigate the current status of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) usage needs among vocational college students from China, explore their relationships with learning engagement and academic resilience, and identify variables associated with GAI usage demand. Methods Using convenience sampling, 3,876 students from five vocational colleges in Sichuan Province were enrolled. Surveys were conducted using the Generative Artificial Intelligence Application Status and Usage Demand Scale, the Learning Engagement Scale, and the Academic Resilience Scale. Results The average GAI needs score among vocational college students was 58.23 ± 12.77. Correlation analysis revealed positive relationships between GAI needs and both learning engagement and academic resilience ( p < 0.01). Multiple linear regression analysis revealed that gender, academic year, availability of GAI learning devices at home, level of GAI understanding, enrollment in GAI-related courses, frequency of active GAI use, student-reported frequency of teachers’ use of GAI in teaching, learning engagement, and academic resilience were independently associated with GAI usage demand (all p < 0.05). The model explained 24.4% of the variance in GAI usage demand [ R 2 = 0.244, adjusted R 2 = 0.241, F (14, 3,861) = 88.932, p < 0.001]. Conclusion Vocational college students’ GAI usage demand was slightly above the theoretical midpoint of the scale. Greater GAI usage demand was independently associated with male gender, earlier academic year, better availability of GAI learning devices at home, a higher level of GAI understanding, enrollment in GAI-related courses, more frequent active GAI use, more frequent student-reported teachers’ use of GAI in teaching, higher learning engagement, and greater academic resilience. Because of the cross-sectional design, these findings should be interpreted as associations rather than causal relationships.

items.title: Open Benchmark of AI Impact on Humans (ImpactBench): an expert-guided, open platform for the holistic evaluation of AI impact on humans
items.abstract: The present work is concerned with how to measure, at scale, the multi-dimensional impact of generative AI models on the individuals who use them. In service of this goal, we introduce the Open Benchmark of AI Impact on Humans, or ImpactBench. Our iterable and expert-guided platform evaluates whether model behaviors support or undermine an individual's wellbeing across psychological, physical, and social domains. ImpactBench translates constructs from domain experts and existing benchmarks into metrics that are grounded in actual model behavior. Success on these metrics occurs either when a model promotes expert-defined desirable behaviors or avoids identified harms. Models are evaluated against these metrics in simulated multi-turn conversations using matched teen and adult scenarios. The conversations are then scored by an LLM judge and verified through reliability audits and human expert review. The current suite delivers 809 metrics drawn from 26 benchmarks. We evaluated ten frontier LLMs against these metrics across 48,540 conversations. Our results indicate that models promoted desirable behaviors in 68.7% of evaluations, but avoided harms in only 53.1%. Majority expert ratings agreed with the automated judge in 83.3% of reviewed cases (Cohen's Kappa = 0.667). Results are released through a public platform that keep aggregate scores traceable to the underlying metrics and transcripts. ImpactBench is intended as evolving infrastructure for independent, transparent evaluation of generative AI's multi-dimensional impact on humans.

items.title: Organisational culture and technology acceptance as catalysts for artificial intelligence adoption towards human resource management effectiveness in Thailand’s industrial hubs
items.abstract: Orientation: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly important in human resource management (HRM), particularly in Thailand’s Eastern Economic Corridor (EEC), a rapidly developing industrial and economic zone. Identifying the key factors that influence AI adoption can help organisations improve the effectiveness of their HRM practices. Research purpose: To test how organisational culture, technology acceptance (TA) and technology readiness (TR) are associated with AI use in HRM use of technology (UT), and how UT is associated with HRM effectiveness (EF), including UT’s mediating role. Motivation for the study: Despite strong promotion of AI for HRM efficiency, limited evidence explains which organisational and behavioural factors most drive AI adoption in industrial estates, particularly in the EEC. Research approach/design and method: A cross-sectional survey of 500 HR professionals in EEC industrial estates (Chachoengsao, Chonburi, Rayong) was analysed using structural equation modelling (SEM) with SmartPLS. Main findings: Organisational culture and TA were positively associated with UT, while TR has no effect. Use of technology showed a strong positive association with EF. Use of technology mediated the relationships of OC and TA on EF, but not TR. Practical/managerial implications: Organisations should strengthen digital-supportive culture and employee TA, as these are more impactful than focusing only on readiness and infrastructure. Contribution/value-add: The study shows OC and TA are stronger drivers of AI-HRM adoption than TR and provides evidence-based guidance for improving HRM effectiveness in the EEC through AI.

items.title: Organizational conditions for OHSM: Comparing managers and OHS representatives in organizations with different gender distribution
items.abstract: Background Organizational conditions are important for conducting occupational health and safety management (OHSM), but there is a lack of knowledge about how such conditions differ between the actors involved in OHSM. Furthermore, previous research shows that working conditions differ between organizations with different gender distributions, but there is a lack of knowledge about what this means for the ability to conduct OHSM. Objective The purpose of this quantitative study is to compare managers’ and occupational health and safety (OHS) representatives’ organizational conditions for conducting OHSM in workplaces with different gender distributions. Methods An electronic questionnaire was completed by 206 managers and 267 OHS representatives in 10 different organizations in Sweden who worked in workplaces with different gender distributions. Analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed to investigate differences between managers and OHS representatives, differences between work units with different gender distributions, and the interaction effect between role and gender distribution. The analysis was adjusted for organizational affiliation. Results Managers rated their organizational conditions for working with occupational health and safety issues more favourably than OHS representatives did, with statistically significant differences in 7 of the 13 Variables examined. No differences were found according to the gender distribution of the workplace. Conclusions In conclusion, this study suggests that managers perceive their organizational conditions for conducting OHSM more favourably than OHS representatives do. Furthermore, perceived organizational conditions for conducting OHSM seem to be similar regardless of the gender distribution in the workplace.

items.title: Organizational value realization from AI-enabled digital health technologies in long-term care: roles of human–AI collaboration and digital literacy
items.abstract: Rapid population aging has intensified pressures on long-term care (LTC) systems, exacerbating workforce shortages and challenges to sustainable healthcare delivery. Although AI-enabled digital health technologies (DHTs) have emerged as promising tools to address these challenges, existing research has focused largely on technology adoption and system use in hospital settings, providing limited understanding of how AI-enabled DHTs realize organizational value and optimize healthcare delivery in LTC organizations. This study aimed to develop and examine an integrated framework for understanding organizational value realization from AI-enabled DHTs in LTC organizations, focusing on the interrelated roles of technological quality, human–AI collaboration, and workforce digital capability. The study also sought to generate evidence to inform healthcare management strategies for optimizing healthcare delivery. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 257 staff from multiple LTC facilities in Taiwan who had used AI-enabled DHTs for at least six months. Data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) and importance-performance map analysis (IPMA). The proposed model explained 77.9% of the variance in perceived organizational value, together with substantial variance in user satisfaction (R 2 = 0.763) and system use (R 2 = 0.652). Human–AI collaboration quality showed the strongest positive association with user satisfaction and was positively associated with system use. User satisfaction was more strongly associated with perceived organizational value than system use. Digital literacy showed significant but differing moderation effects across these relationships. IPMA identified AI explainability, adaptive personalization, system stability, and functional completeness as priority areas for improvement. These findings advance understanding of organizational value realization from AI-enabled DHTs in LTC organizations by highlighting the roles of human–AI collaboration and digital literacy. They underscore the value of explainable, adaptive, and human-centered AI design in supporting positive user experiences with AI-enabled DHTs. Workforce digital literacy may further shape how these technology experiences relate to perceived organizational value. These insights provide evidence to inform healthcare management strategies that align AI system design and workforce development with organizational objectives to support healthcare delivery optimization and sustainable long-term care in aging societies.

items.title: Perceived Value and Adoption Intention of Enterprise AI Solutions in Bangladesh: Integrating the Technology Acceptance Model and Diffusion of Innovations Theory
items.abstract: Enterprise artificial intelligence (AI) adoption is increasingly framed as a value-realisation problem rather than a simple question of whether users are willing to try new technologies. This study examines perceived value and adoption intention for enterprise AI/cloud solutions among technology-oriented respondents in Bangladesh by integrating the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) with Diffusion of Innovations (DOI) theory. Distinct from a conventional predictor-only adoption model, the study specifies a value-realization mechanism in which relative advantage and compatibility shape perceived usefulness, which in turn contributes to adoption intention; direct DOI-to-intention paths are retained to test partial versus full mediation. Innovation adoption readiness is additionally examined as a boundary condition on the usefulness-intention relationship. The supplied database contains 385 complete observations after exclusion of 15 blank rows. Respondents are distributed across students, employed professionals, and self-employed/freelance users, with substantial variation in technology-use frequency and experience. Composite-score path analysis shows that relative advantage and compatibility are positively associated with perceived usefulness (β=.204 and β=.217, respectively; both p<.001). Perceived usefulness is positively associated with adoption intention (β=.119, p=.020), while relative advantage (β=.147, p=.005), compatibility (β=.156, p=.003), and innovation adoption readiness (β=.150, p=.004) also have significant direct associations with adoption intention. Bootstrap indirect effects through perceived usefulness are positive for both relative advantage (ab=.025, 95% CI [.003, .052]) and compatibility (ab=.026, 95% CI [.004, .053]). The usefulness × readiness interaction is not statistically significant (β=.039, p=.447). The findings therefore indicate a partial value-realisation pathway rather than a simple direct-determinants model. The article contributes by linking innovation attributes to the TAM usefulness mechanism in a Bangladesh enterprise-AI context and by showing that readiness operates more clearly as a direct adoption resource than as a moderator of usefulness.

items.title: Personalized GenAI coaching and self-regulation in L2 writing across a nine-week active-control study
items.abstract: Introduction Personalized rationale is an explanation of why a metacognitive strategy is relevant to a learner’s current writing. This study compared a personalized GenAI coaching package with template-based adaptive metacognitive prompting (AMP) in a nine-week randomized study of Chinese EFL undergraduates. Methods Ninety-two participants completed pretest, posttest, and three-week delayed posttest assessments. Both conditions used the same Doubao LLM, interface, and trigger infrastructure. The AMP-Agent condition combined an essay-specific observation, personalized rationale, and an open-ended question; the AMP condition used template prompts. Results Analyses of questionnaire item responses found Group × Time interactions for self-regulated learning (SRL; p = 0.019) and GenAI dependency ( p = 0.010), which also survived a retrospective Holm sensitivity correction across the three total outcomes. The SRL total contrasts at posttest and delayed posttest did not survive Bonferroni correction across time points. Self-reported GenAI dependency questionnaire scores were lower in the AMP-Agent group at both later assessments after this correction. Evidence for different writing-score trajectories was insufficient (interaction p = 0.101). None of five highlighted behavioral transitions survived correction across 20 transition comparisons. Discussion The findings support a difference in self-reported regulation and dependency trajectories between the two prompting packages, while leaving the contribution of rationale alone, sustained writing benefits, and psychological mechanisms unresolved.

items.title: Pre-service physics teachers as designers of AI-based pedagogical infrastructure: supporting metacognitive learning in STEM classrooms
items.abstract: This study explored how pre-service physics teachers design artificial intelligence (AI)-based pedagogical infrastructure to support metacognitive learning in STEM classrooms. A qualitative interpretive design was employed with 30 pre-service physics teachers enrolled in a physics teacher education program at a university in Kazakhstan. Following two preparatory workshops, participants developed, tested, and refined AI-supported STEM lesson scenarios over 12 weeks. Testing involved peer-based micro-teaching with fellow pre-service teachers acting in simulated student roles; no school students participated. Data comprised individual semi-structured interviews, lesson plans, AI interaction scenarios, prompt sequences, and reflective notes and were examined using reflexive thematic analysis. Six interrelated themes were identified: designing AI-supported STEM lessons; supporting metacognitive regulation and formative assessment; aligning AI use with the physics curriculum and STEM objectives; preserving student agency and ensuring responsible AI use; developing teacher design agency; and addressing conditions for sustainable implementation. Participants' designs generally shifted from using AI to generate ready-made materials toward integrating it more purposefully into structured learning sequences. Pedagogically meaningful scenarios required learners to formulate an initial prediction or solution before consulting AI, verify AI-generated responses using physical laws, calculations, experiments, and reliable sources, and reflect on and revise their reasoning. Reported challenges included inaccurate AI responses, preparation time, unequal access to digital resources, technical difficulties, and variations in the quality of Kazakh- and Russian-language outputs. The findings highlight the importance of preparing pre-service physics teachers for subject-specific, ethically responsible, and pedagogically grounded AI integration. They illustrate design practices intended to scaffold planning, monitoring, scientific verification, evaluation, and reflection. However, the findings concern participants' pedagogical designs and professional perceptions and do not establish improvements in school students' metacognitive regulation or learning outcomes.

items.title: Redefining creativity in AI era: Bloom’s taxonomy framework and peer interaction elevate higher-order thinking skills
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is transforming cognitive learning by reshaping pedagogical models and raising questions about its impact on higher-order thinking. AI-driven personalized learning improves knowledge acquisition, but its effect on creativity remains largely unexplored. Most research emphasizes content delivery over cognitive engagement, which leaves gaps in understanding how AI influences deeper learning processes. This study investigates how ChatGPT-enabled personalized learning, framed through Bloom's Taxonomy, influences creative thinking among Indonesian higher education students, considering the moderating role of peer interaction. Using SEM via Smart-PLS 4.1, data from 533 Indonesian students reveal that personalized learning strengthens both lower-order cognitive skills-such as remembering, understanding, and applying-and higher-order functions, including analyzing, evaluating, and creating, which are essential for creativity. Among these, analyzing and creating have the strongest impact on creative thinking. Peer interaction selectively moderates this relationship, significantly enhancing creativity in tasks involving creation, while its effect on other cognitive functions remains limited. This study introduces a dynamic framework that integrates personalized learning, Bloom's Taxonomy, and peer collaboration, offering new insights into how tailored cognitive processes and selective peer engagement drive creativity in learning environments.

items.title: Redesigning collaborative teaching for human–AI partnership: a phase-based AI-constraint design principle in higher education
items.abstract: Generative AI is now a routine presence in higher-education classrooms, shifting the operative question from whether to permit its use toward when and how access should be structured within a learning activity. This paper reports a design-based research programme examining phase-based AI constraints, deliberately restricting AI access to specific phases of a collaborative teaching method rather than permitting or prohibiting it wholesale, as a design principle for structuring human and AI contributions within collaborative learning activities. The wider DBR programme examined AI-augmented designs across six collaborative teaching methods, administered repeatedly to five student groups over two academic years; the phase-based AI-constraint principle reported here as DP1 was developed through, and its evidence anchored in, Think-Pair-Share, with the other five methods contributing broader DBR context rather than independent confirmatory evidence. Its strongest evidence comes from an AI-free Think phase within Think-Pair-Share, replicated across three independent student groups spanning three degree programs, where learners consistently endorsed the AI-free phase as appropriate; this endorsement pattern was typically the highest-scoring item on its questionnaire. This design itself resulted from an earlier design cycle within the same programme: an initial administration permitting AI access during this phase prompted redesign after the instructor's classroom observation indicated that independent reflection was being displaced by AI-mediated responses. We treat this endorsement as an empirical finding, not as a direct assessment of the quality or originality of what learners produced, and not as evidence that the phase in fact protects independent cognitive engagement; that stronger claim is a theoretically motivated proposition this study does not test, and we frame DP1 accordingly across three explicit levels: an empirical endorsement finding, a transferable design principle of differentiating AI access by activity phase rather than deciding it once for a whole activity, and an untested theoretical proposition about the cognitive mechanism this differentiation may support. A complementary, independent stakeholder strand surveyed higher-education professionals at a practitioner festival session, offering a modest, exploratory social-validity signal: the phase-based procedure itself was almost universally endorsed, while personal adoption intention was somewhat more reserved. An exploratory qualitative coding of practitioners' open responses showed only slight inter-coder reliability ( κ =0.17), so we do not use these responses to derive additional design principles, retaining only one response on function-based AI restriction as an illustrative example. The study is exploratory and formative, without a no-AI control condition or random assignment, and we frame its claims as design-principle evidence within a design-based research programme rather than as causal effect estimates. Anchored in independently replicated student endorsement data from Think-Pair-Share and supplemented by a practitioner social-validity signal, phase-based AI constraints offer higher-education instructors an actionable, low-friction design principle, one we expect to be conceptually transferable to other collaborative teaching methods, though this transfer remains to be empirically demonstrated.

items.title: Reliable AI at Scale: Data Engineering for the Intelligent Systems Era — Sample Chapters (Chapters 1 and 4)
items.abstract: This free sample edition contains two full chapters of "Reliable AI at Scale: Data Engineering for the Intelligent Systems Era," a book about the data systems artificial intelligence actually stands on. The book's argument: AI systems are data-intensive systems, and their failures are data failures. Included chapters: - Chapter 1: The Data-Intensive AI Stack — the book's thesis and the seven-layer frame (ingestion, storage, processing, orchestration, quality, observability, authority) every later chapter deepens. - Chapter 4: Stream Processing and Real-Time ML — event time, watermarks, and exactly-once semantics, then the ML turn: real-time features, point-in-time correctness, and training-serving skew. The full book has eleven chapters: 1. The Data-Intensive AI Stack 2. Ingestion at Scale: From Events to Actions 3. Storage for Intelligent Systems 4. Stream Processing and Real-Time ML 5. Consistency, Correctness, and Data Quality 6. Feature Engineering and Feature Platforms 7. Orchestration, Sagas, and Long-Running Workflows 8. Federated and Privacy-Preserving Learning 9. MLOps, Feedback Loops, and Continuous Intelligence 10. Autonomous Agents as Data-Intensive Systems 11. Operating AI Systems in Production: Reliability, Observability, Security Each chapter is written to stand alone: an opening production-failure scenario (a fictional composite), the principles that explain it, the architectural patterns that prevent it, trade-offs, and a "what to build first" checklist. About the author: Sai Prasad Veluru is a Senior Software Engineer at Immihub, where he works on distributed systems and production AI. Over eleven years in the industry — including engineering roles at Apple, JPMorgan Chase, and Visa — he has designed and operated high-throughput ingestion platforms, real-time streaming systems, and cloud-native data infrastructure, and he now builds agentic AI systems engineered to survive production. He is the author of twenty-five publications on distributed systems, stream processing, federated learning, and production AI, cited more than 150 times, and he serves as a judge at HackMIT and MHacks. items.title: Research on AI-Assisted Mathematics Teaching in Primary and Secondary Schools (2022-2026)
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support mathematics teaching, yet research examining its instructional effects and implementation conditions in primary and secondary schools remains fragmented. This study reviewed published research on AI-assisted mathematics teaching between 2022 and 2026. Relevant records were retrieved from the Web of Science database using topic searches for AI and mathematics education. Of 262 initially identified records, 44 studies met the stated inclusion criteria and were included in a thematic synthesis. Three principal research areas emerged: instructional effects, factors influencing effectiveness, and strategies for improvement. The reviewed studies generally reported favourable outcomes for students’ mathematics achievement, conceptual understanding, interest, motivation and classroom engagement, although some interventions produced limited or inconsistent benefits. AI tools also supported teachers’ lesson planning, resource preparation, assessment, learning diagnosis and instructional decision-making. Reported outcomes depended on teacher-related factors, including AI literacy, attitudes and pedagogical competencies; student-related factors, including self-regulation, digital literacy and interaction patterns; technological factors, particularly accuracy, usability and personalisation; and contextual factors, including infrastructure, family support and educational resources. Suggested improvements included professional development, teacher-led implementation, clearer ethical and data-governance arrangements, and the development of more reliable mathematics-specific tools. The findings indicate that AI can provide useful instructional support, but its effectiveness depends on appropriate educational integration and local conditions. Longitudinal classroom research is needed to clarify sustained outcomes and the interaction of these factors.

items.title: Responsible and Trustworthy Agentic AI: Governance, Assurance, Explainability, Controllability, and Human Oversight: A Comprehensive Survey
items.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence combines goal-directed reasoning, planning, memory, tool use, adaptation and multi-agent coordination with the ability to affect external systems. This capability raises problems of authorization, safety, human oversight, accountability and the evidence required to justify reliance. This non-systematic integrative survey distinguishes AI ethics, responsible AI, governance, trustworthiness, assurance, explainability, security and controllability; synthesizes preventive, detective, corrective, human-based and agent-based controls; and compares responsibility and oversight arrangements across the agent lifecycle. Building on established governance and meaningful-human-control research, it proposes an authority-control-assurance-accountability mapping that connects normative requirements to delegated decision rights, enforceable controls, observable evidence, escalation conditions and identifiable organizational owners. Two fictional cases illustrate the proposed mapping for document access and software changes. The framework is a conceptual synthesis rather than an empirically validated assurance standard. The survey identifies limitations of supervisory-agent independence, long-horizon explanation, dynamic authorization and continuous re-assurance, and specifies research questions for future evaluation.

items.title: Review on unobtrusive estimation of team processes underlying team situation awareness: shared mental models and team coordination
items.abstract: Introduction Team situation awareness (SA) is essential for effective team performance. Yet, current methods rely on potentially biased self-reports and obtrusive tools such as task probes. Objective, unobtrusive, and continuous methods for monitoring team SA could support its improvement. In contrast to individual SA, unobtrusive measures of team SA have not been systematically reviewed. Because team SA is an umbrella concept, we adapted a framework proposed by Salmon et al., identifying two components that can potentially be measured unobtrusively: shared mental models (SMMs) and team coordination. This systematic review examines behavioural and physiological technologies that may enable unobtrusive measurement of these components. Methods We conducted a systematic literature review of studies investigating behavioural technologies, such as verbal communication and eye-tracking, and physiological technologies, such as electroencephalography, for unobtrusive measurement of team SMMs and coordination. We searched Web of Science (May and July 2025) for relevant literature published between 2000 and 2025. We included peer-reviewed articles published in English. In total, 19 studies addressing team SMMs and 33 addressing team coordination were included. We extracted sample and team size, task environment, operationalisation of team SMMs and coordination, and their relationship with unobtrusive measures. Results Cardiac measures (42%) and verbal communication (47%) were most popular for estimating team SMMs, while functional near-infrared spectroscopy (27%) and cardiac measures (30%) were most popular for estimating team coordination. Interpersonal synchrony—the temporal contiguity and interdependence of physiological and/or behavioural activity between teammates—was applied in 70% of team coordination studies. Studies covered diverse tasks and settings, from laboratory-based cognitive tasks and controlled physical tasks to real-world environments, including surgery. Various methods were used to operationalise SMMs and coordination, including participant experience, expert assessment, and self-reports. Discussion Findings suggest that team SMMs and coordination cannot be measured as single, unified constructs using one unobtrusive measure. Instead, different measures may provide information about specific aspects of these processes. Future research should begin with task analysis to identify relevant aspects of team SA and derive appropriate measures for the specific task environment. Task-related behavioural actions also represent a potentially valuable, yet often overlooked, category of unobtrusive measures. A key limitation is the substantial variation in how SMMs and coordination were operationalised and measured, making direct comparisons difficult. Future work should investigate how identified measures relate directly to team SA using validated measures.

items.title: Same Claim, Different Interpretations: How LLM Agents Resolve Ambiguity in Scientific Claims
items.abstract: Co-scientists and agentic scientific claim verifiers are increasingly used to assess claims across the sciences. Natural-language scientific claims, written for human experts, are often underspecified and so admit several defensible interpretations. Such verifiers usually pick one, often tacitly, and benchmarks score their verdicts against expert labels without recording the expert's interpretation or the verifier's in a comparable form. This leads to disagreements with expert labels that cannot be traced to the evidence or the interpretation, and to compute spent on unchecked interpretations. We introduce Claim Cards to make such interpretations explicit in the reasoning itself. A Claim Card records a verifier's interpretation as nine fields before evidence gathering, each marked stated, inferred, or default. To test whether an agent's interpretation can change its verdict, we ran a GPT-5.4 agent five times on each of 60 expert-labeled materials-science and biomedical claims with a card, without one, and with one card frozen across runs (900 runs). Over 40% of card fields were not marked stated, and a card added about a tenth to a run's GPT-5.4 tokens and time without measurably changing agreement with expert labels. The agent's own interpretations varied between runs, although within a claim this variation did not measurably track the verdict. A deliberate change to one field of the frozen card, however, making the quantifier universal or the threshold for support stricter, changed the verdict on about a third of the claims, against about one in seven expected by chance (p < 0.001 for each edit). On 24 materials-science claims run with computational tools, the stricter threshold also changed what the agent asked those tools to compute. We therefore argue that verdicts should be reported with their interpretations and that benchmarks could publish the interpretation behind each label.

items.title: SCIENTIFIC AND METHODOLOGICAL FOUNDATIONS FOR IMPLEMENTING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TECHNOLOGIES IN THE CONTEXT OF DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION
items.abstract: This thesis examines the scientific and methodological foundations for integrating artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into organizational processes under digital transformation. Drawing on research in information systems, organizational AI readiness, software engineering, and risk management, it identifies the conditions under which AI adoption can generate measurable value. The analysis distinguishes technological deployment from organizational transformation and considers data governance, model selection, validation, human oversight, and continuous monitoring as interdependent implementation requirements. A conceptual, stage-based approach is proposed for connecting organizational objectives with technical design and operational performance. The contribution is methodological and analytical; no independent experimental outcomes or unverified performance improvements are claimed.

items.title: Self-reported understanding and attitudes of healthcare workers and caregivers toward artificial intelligence in pediatric healthcare in a children’s hospital in China: a cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Objective To investigate the self-reported understanding and attitudes of healthcare workers and caregivers toward the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in pediatric healthcare in a children’s specialty hospital, and to compare differences between the two groups. Methods This single-center cross-sectional questionnaire survey was conducted at Fujian Children’s Hospital from January 2026 to June 2026. A self-designed questionnaire was used to assess healthcare workers’ and caregivers’ self-reported understanding, trust, risk perception, and willingness to accept AI applications in pediatric healthcare. Respondents were divided into groups according to their identity. Categorical variables were compared using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test, while continuous variables were compared using the independent-samples t test or the Mann–Whitney U test. Results A total of 261 respondents were included, comprising 159 caregivers and 102 healthcare workers. Healthcare workers had a higher level of self-reported understanding and a higher frequency of use of AI applications in pediatric healthcare than caregivers ( p < 0.01); however, they also showed stronger perceptions of data security risks ( p < 0.001). Caregivers reported greater trust in AI-assisted medical decision-making than healthcare workers ( p < 0.001). Most respondents believed that AI could not replace pediatric healthcare workers, with no statistically significant difference between the two groups ( p = 0.166). Regarding potential advantages, healthcare workers were more likely to agree that AI could reduce human error ( p < 0.001). Regarding potential limitations, healthcare workers expressed greater concern about the risks of misdiagnosis, lack of humanistic care, and data privacy and security issues ( p < 0.001). Conclusion In this single-center children’s specialty hospital, healthcare workers reported greater self-rated understanding and more frequent use of AI, together with stronger awareness of several potential risks, whereas caregivers showed greater trust in AI-assisted medical decision-making despite lower self-rated understanding. These findings should be interpreted cautiously and require confirmation in larger multicenter studies before being generalized to broader populations in China.
